rule: accumulated MIXED Track-B channels, ranked by |alone-AUC - .5| on FIT+MINE only
selected_parents: Count of enumerated evaluation settings and resource markers
Extent of formal notation and mathematical vocabulary

candidates.criterion: Count of enumerated evaluation settings and resource markers
candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 by counting or estimating how many distinct evaluation settings and resource markers the abstract enumerates. Count mentions of: named or counted datasets or benchmarks; tasks; languages; domains; model architectures or model families; model sizes or parameter counts; transfer, zero-shot, or cross-lingual settings; numbers of baselines compared; and explicit scale statements such as compute used, number of runs, or number of human raters. 0 = the abstract names no evaluation setting at all. 2 = one setting is named. 5 = roughly three or four distinct settings or counts are named. 8 = five to eight are named, or explicit large counts appear. 10 = the abstract enumerates many settings, or states large counts across several of these categories. This is explicitly NOT a quality judgement. Do not decide whether the coverage is adequate, necessary, convincing, or excessive; do not consider whether anything informative was learned in those settings; do not consider whether the comparisons were controlled. Score only how much enumeration is present in the text.
candidates.upstream_parent: surface carrier of bank criterion: Evaluation breadth

candidates.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract contains theorem, proof, bound, assumption, equation, or mathematically formal terminology; judge formalism extent only, not rigor, correctness, or research value.

Score 0-10 how many currently-fashionable subfield buzzwords appear in the abstract (e.g., 'GPT', 'in-context learning', 'diffusion', 'Transformer', 'large language model', 'foundation model'). 0 = no such terms appear; 10 = the abstract is dense with such terms throughout. Do not judge whether the use of these terms is warranted, accurate, or central to the contribution -- score only the raw presence of this vocabulary.

candidates.criterion: Extent of formal notation and mathematical vocabulary
candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 the raw extent of mathematically formal vocabulary and notation in the abstract text. Count or estimate the presence of: words such as theorem, lemma, proposition, corollary, proof, bound, convergence, rate, assumption, regularity, convexity, optimality, complexity, and similar formal-mathematical vocabulary; and any inline mathematical notation such as Greek letters, single-letter variable names, subscripts or superscripts, norms, expectations, probability symbols, big-O expressions, inequalities, or displayed formulas. 0 = the abstract contains none of these markers at all. 3 = one or two isolated markers. 7 = markers recur in several sentences. 10 = the abstract is dense with such vocabulary and notation from start to finish. This is explicitly NOT a quality judgement. Do not consider whether the formalism is correct, rigorous, necessary, well used, or informative; do not consider whether the paper actually proves anything; do not consider whether the notation is defined. Score only how much of this vocabulary and notation is present on the page.
candidates.upstream_parent: surface carrier of bank criterion: Formalism density

candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text lists many datasets, tasks, domains, architectures, baselines, or experimental settings; judge the breadth of enumeration only, not whether the evaluation is adequate or persuasive.

Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract claims coverage across multiple datasets, languages, domains, tasks, architectures, or transfer settings; judge breadth of described coverage only, not whether it is adequate or convincing.
Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses theorem, proof, bound, convergence, asymptotic, or formal mathematical-guarantee language; judge only extent, not correctness or importance.

Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses equations, asymptotic notation, named theorems, proofs, bounds, optimization conditions, or other formal mathematical language; judge amount only, not whether the formalism is rigorous or valuable.
How much does the abstract name canonical datasets, benchmarks, architectures, standard methods, or well-known prior authors? Score only visible ecosystem references, not the importance of the work.

candidates.criterion: Density of specific quantified result figures
candidates.instruction: Rate 0-10 the density of explicitly quantified outcome figures in the text. Count numerals attached to results: percentages, absolute metric values (accuracy, AP, mIoU, FID, MAE), speedup or reduction factors (for example five-fold, two to three orders of magnitude), parameter, FLOP or batch-size counts, wall-clock times, and dataset sizes. Anchors: 0 = no such numerals anywhere; 3 = one figure; 5 = two or three; 8 = four or five; 10 = six or more distinct quantified figures, several carried to one or two decimal places. Score PRESENCE AND DENSITY of numbers only. Do not assess whether the numbers are large, impressive, fairly compared, correctly computed, or whether the gains would matter to anyone.

Rate from 0 to 10 how much the abstract advertises code, pretrained models, datasets, repositories, or reproducibility artifacts; judge the presence of availability statements only, not whether the artifacts are useful or the research is sound.

Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit language promising or linking code, models, datasets, configurations, or other research artifacts; judge only the presence of release signaling, not whether the artifacts are useful or real.

Score how many specific, checkable numeric results (percentages, deltas, counts, timings) the abstract reports, independent of how positive or well-supported they are. A 10 packs multiple precise figures (e.g., '10.9% improvement', '5-fold reduction', '76 minutes'). A 0 reports only qualitative adjectives ('significant', 'considerable', 'remarkable') with no numbers at all.

Score 0-10 how explicitly the abstract states that code, data, or trained models will be or are being released (e.g., a repository URL, 'code is available at...', 'we release our implementation'). 0 = no release statement of any kind; 10 = an explicit, specific release statement naming a repository. Do not judge whether releasing code says anything about the work's quality -- score only whether the statement is textually present.

candidates.criterion: Density of quantified benchmark results in text
candidates.instruction: Rate 0-10 the density of concrete quantitative results stated in the abstract: numerals, percentage gains, absolute metric values, benchmark deltas, parameter counts, FLOP counts, speedup factors and named leaderboard figures. 0 = no numbers reported at all; 3 = one vague quantified claim; 6 = two or three precise figures; 10 = many precise figures woven through several sentences. Count how much quantified reporting is present on the surface. Do not judge whether the numbers are large, impressive, credible, correctly obtained or well chosen, and do not reward or penalise the absence of numbers.

Score whether the abstract explicitly states that code, models, or data will be or are publicly released. A 10 states a concrete release (e.g., a GitHub link or explicit 'code is available'). A 0 makes no mention of release or reproducibility artifacts.

Score from 0 (absent) to 10 (highly prominent) the extent to which the abstract contains an explicit URL to a code repository (e.g., GitHub) or explicitly states that code is open-sourced. Do not judge the quality or usefulness of the code, only the presence of the repository mention.
Score 0-10 for how much the abstract introduces named methods, abbreviations, and component labels; judge only extent, not whether the naming is useful or technically good.

candidates.criterion: Sheer expository volume of the abstract body
candidates.instruction: Read only the abstract text and rate 0-10 how much total expository volume is present. Anchors: 0 = title only, or a single sentence of body text; 3 = roughly two to four sentences; 6 = one standard paragraph of about eight to twelve sentences; 10 = a long multi-part abstract of fifteen or more sentences covering several elaborated sub-topics. Count sentences, clauses, enumerated sub-points and number of distinct sub-topics touched. You are measuring QUANTITY OF TEXT ONLY. Do not judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the writing is clear or informative, or whether a short abstract is terse-and-confident versus thin. Longer is not better and shorter is not better; report extent only.
Rate from 0 (very brief) to 10 (very long) how much text, sentence count, and elaboration the abstract contains; judge extent only, not whether the additional detail is good or useful.
Score 0-10 for the extent of fluent grammar, consistent terminology, smooth transitions, and carefully standardized prose; judge only textual polish, not research quality.

How much does the abstract exhibit highly polished grammar, smooth transitions, standardized abstract structure, and publication-template fluency? Score only surface editing quality, not research quality.

Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how much specialized mathematical/symbolic notation appears (inline formulas, Greek letters, subscripts/superscripts, big-O/tilde-O expressions, set/space notation like R^d). Score 0 if the text is plain prose with no symbolic notation, and 10 if the text is dense with symbolic expressions throughout. Do NOT judge whether the mathematics is correct, rigorous, or important -- score only how much symbolic notation is visibly present in the text.

candidates.criterion: Rhetorical framing as adjudicating a field debate
candidates.instruction: Score whether the abstract explicitly frames itself as resolving an open question or tension in prior literature, using a direct question or an explicit 'prior work suggests X, but...' setup, versus simply stating 'we propose method M for task T' without any such framing device. A 10 opens with an explicit posed question or named tension the paper will resolve. A 0 states its contribution directly with no debate-framing device.

Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how strongly the text makes an explicit claim to being first, novel-in-priority, or unprecedented (e.g., 'we are the first to...', 'for the first time', 'to the best of our knowledge, ... is the first'). Score 0 if no such priority claim appears, and 10 if the text makes an emphatic, explicit priority claim. Do NOT judge whether the priority claim is actually true or historically accurate -- score only whether this rhetorical claim is textually present.

candidates.criterion: Named large-scale computing infrastructure or hardware mentions
candidates.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text names specific large-scale or branded computing infrastructure, hardware, or vendor platforms (e.g. a named cloud TPU/GPU pod, a named trusted-hardware enclave, a named corporate code namespace) as part of describing the experiments. Score only the presence/specificity of such named infrastructure mentions; do NOT judge whether that infrastructure was necessary or whether the resulting research is good.

Score 10 if the paper proposes complex, fine-grained mechanisms for dynamically routing or mixing information between specific architectural sub-components (e.g., layers, image regions). Score 0 if it uses standard, monolithic end-to-end processing.
